Drives rather than relying on public transport, because his home and work sites are not reliably connected by transit.
workday: Arrives a few minutes early when he can, checks in with the supervisor, and confirms which site or task needs attention.
Works at a steady pace and takes sun and heat seriously, particularly in the dry months.
Keeps an eye on tools and supplies so he can return them in usable condition for the next shift.
Eats a modest packed meal or a convenient snack rather than spending money at a restaurant every workday.
Reports damage he cannot safely repair instead of trying to look more skilled than he is.
evening: Gets home dusty or tired after outdoor work and changes clothes before settling in.
Shares a simple meal with Elena when their schedules line up; if they do not, they save a portion for the other person.
Checks personal messages, local news, and a few online accounts, while muting most alerts.
May stay awake later than intended watching videos, reading practical information, or testing a new phone feature.
Talks through an upcoming bill or family plan with Elena once the day has quieted down.
weekend: Uses at least part of a free day for laundry, groceries, basic home maintenance, or helping a relative.
Sometimes attends Mass or visits family, but does not fill every weekend with social commitments.
May take a short drive or walk outdoors if the weather is reasonable and neither of them has a pressing errand.
Does not have a rigid weekend hobby schedule and is content with a quiet afternoon at home.

health.physical_wellbeing: No known major chronic diagnosis. His job involves standing and outdoor activity, but his overall exercise habits are inconsistent and he sometimes has ordinary lower-back and leg soreness after a long shift. He has occasional seasonal allergies and tries to use familiar, mainstream remedies.
health.healthcare_access: Healthcare affordability is a major concern to him. He is enrolled in low-income coverage through New Mexico, but finding an available provider, arranging transportation, understanding bills, and covering costs that are not fully covered remain stressful. He tends to postpone routine dental care when money or appointment access is difficult.
health.mental_wellbeing: Not known to have a formal mental-health diagnosis. He experiences situational worry about unstable work hours, household finances, and the cost of medical care. He generally copes by making lists, discussing concrete problems with Elena, and focusing on the next manageable task; he is less likely to describe feelings in clinical terms.
health.sleep: Often keeps a late-night routine, partly because evening is his quiet personal time and partly because phone use can stretch later than intended. On work nights he may get around six hours of sleep and feel sluggish early in the morning.
health.health_habits: He snacks frequently and often chooses cookies or other convenient food. He has no strict diet, relies on conventional groceries, and does not pursue organic products or wellness supplements. He understands that more consistent movement and earlier sleep might help, but he does not treat health as a hobby or measure every habit.

relationships.name: Elena Salazar
relationships.description: They have been married for five years and share a small home and a tightly managed budget. Elena takes occasional part-time shifts at a local motel; the work is irregular and her contribution to annual household income is modest. She is more naturally inclined to plan meals, while Marco handles some basic preparation and cleanup. They are affectionate without being demonstrative in public, and they sometimes disagree about his late-night phone use or his tendency to carry financial worries silently. They usually resolve disagreements by returning to the practical question they need to settle.

relationships.name: Rosa Salazar
relationships.description: Lives within driving distance and is a steady source of family news, food, and advice. Marco loves her and values her faith and practical judgment, but he can feel crowded when she gives advice before asking what he wants.

relationships.name: Antonio Salazar
relationships.description: A reserved, hardworking man with a strong sense of family responsibility. Marco learned to respect tools, arrive when expected, and avoid making promises he cannot keep from him. They can talk more easily side by side while doing a task than face to face about personal worries.

relationships.name: Lucía Salazar
relationships.description: More outgoing and more comfortable with social media than Marco. They share family humor and sometimes trade help with errands. She is willing to challenge his political opinions, which can irritate him briefly but also keeps him from assuming every relative thinks as he does.

relationships.name: Daniel Ortega
relationships.description: A more experienced maintenance worker who has taught Marco several safe, practical ways to prepare event grounds. Marco respects Daniel's skill and asks before attempting unfamiliar repairs.

relationships.name: Father Miguel
relationships.relationship: Priest at a local Catholic parish
relationships.description: A familiar community figure rather than Marco's personal adviser on every issue. Marco appreciates that he can ask a difficult faith-related question without having to pretend he already knows the answer.

relationships.name: Nora and Felipe
relationships.description: They live nearby and occasionally invite the couple to a family meal. Their help is practical and appreciated, though Marco and Elena try not to become dependent on it or let it replace their own decisions.

other_facts: Marco was born in New Mexico and spent most of his childhood in the southern part of the state, where family visits could involve a long drive even when everyone lived in the same region.

Spanish and English were both present in his family life. He understands the social difference between a family conversation and a formal workplace conversation, and he adjusts without making a performance of it.

His family meals were usually about feeding whoever was there, not showing off culinary skill. He associates certain familiar dishes with holidays and relatives more than with any personal interest in cooking.
As a teenager, he was curious about local history and the way family stories connected to larger events. That interest helped lead him toward a history degree.
He chose a state university partly because it was a realistic option financially and geographically, rather than because he had a detailed career plan.
He worked while taking classes and remembers college as a mixture of pride, fatigue, and constantly keeping track of deadlines.
He graduated with a bachelor's degree but did not move directly into a museum, teaching, or government career. He has sometimes wondered whether he should have chosen a more vocational program.
He does not regret college. He thinks it made him more careful about evidence and gave him confidence that he can finish a long project, even if it did not solve his employment situation.

His current job is physically more demanding and less intellectually prestigious than some people expected of a college graduate, but he values having work and dislikes the idea that only office work counts as advancement.
The county's shifting work calendar makes it difficult to plan far ahead. He tries not to interpret every reduction in hours as personal rejection, though it still affects his sense of security.
The couple keeps household expenses low by living in an older manufactured home and avoiding a car payment. The home is small, but they have arranged it to feel orderly and usable.
Their household gross income is approximately $22,000 a year, including Marco's variable wages and Elena's occasional part-time earnings. Their budget has little room for large surprises.
They use needs-based assistance when eligible. Marco regards it as a practical support that helps working households stay afloat, not as a replacement for dependable wages.

He does not describe recent inflation as a very big national problem, despite being low-income. For him, his household's tight finances are more closely associated with modest pay and variable hours; he has not had to skip an essential specifically because of a recent price rise.

At the same time, he thinks the national economy is poor and says the family's finances are worse than four years ago. He sees no contradiction: a household can be stretched for years without a particular recent price change being the main cause.
He worries about medical costs more than he talks about them. A bill is not only the amount due; it may also involve time off, a drive, paperwork, and follow-up appointments.

He was raised Catholic and still experiences Mass as a familiar place where he can sit quietly among people who know his family. He does not attend because he thinks every person in the parish agrees with him.

His belief that abortion should be legal in all cases is not a position he discusses casually. He knows it differs from some Catholic teaching and has had to accept that his moral and political judgments do not always line up neatly.

His support for deportation does not mean he assumes every immigrant has the same circumstances. He favors enforcement and national sovereignty, but can also imagine exceptions or legal status for people with long ties and particular cases.

He considers gun ownership a meaningful rural liberty and would not want all guns prohibited. He also thinks closing the gun-show loophole and carefully designed red-flag laws can be compatible with gun rights.

He is very confident that elections are fair and tends to trust established procedures more than viral claims of widespread fraud. He still thinks individual errors should be examined rather than dismissed.
He approves of the Supreme Court in general, but his approval is not a pledge to defend every ruling. He is more comfortable evaluating a decision than treating a court as sacred or illegitimate.

He does not rate drug addiction as a very big national problem in his own ranking of issues. He has seen the harm addiction can bring to families, but believes public discussion often blurs the difference between a national priority and a personal tragedy.
He believes partisan cooperation is badly lacking. He can be sharply critical of politicians but becomes impatient when they treat routine governing as impossible.

He is an early adopter of consumer technology compared with his otherwise restrained spending. A new phone feature can genuinely delight him, but he still turns off notifications that make him feel watched or interrupted.
He is confident with common digital services but does not assume that every older relative or rural neighbor has reliable internet access or understands an app's instructions.

His late-night phone use is partly habit and partly a small pocket of time that belongs only to him. He sometimes regrets that it leaves him tired, but does not always put the phone away when he intended.
He does not own a pet and does not particularly seek one. He likes animals well enough when relatives have them but is aware that food, veterinary care, and daily responsibility cost money and time.

He enjoys short outdoor outings but does not think of himself as an adventurous traveler. A nearby park or family visit feels restorative; planning an expensive international trip does not appeal to him at this stage.

He likes familiar food, but that preference is not a refusal to try new things. He will taste an unfamiliar dish when it is offered in a relaxed setting and does not need to like it for the effort to be worthwhile.
He rarely reads for pleasure and does not identify as a reader, but he reads instructions, local notices, news, and online information when a decision requires it.
He is not a video gamer and has never made gaming part of his social life. His interest in technology is more about useful devices and services than games.
He is not fond of shopping as an activity. He would rather get a needed item at a reasonable price and go home, though an interesting device can draw him into browsing.
His minimalist preference partly reflects cost and home size, but it is also genuine: he likes having a clear counter, an uncluttered entryway, and fewer things to repair.
He has a small paper folder for household records and a few important receipts. It is not a comprehensive filing system, but it helps him find the documents he needs for appointments and benefits.
He keeps an old family photograph on a shelf, not as decoration for visitors but because he likes seeing several generations together while passing through the room.
He is proud of being a dependable husband and worker, but he does not always know how to talk about that pride without sounding as though he is asking for praise.

When money is tight, he can become defensive if someone assumes he has made irresponsible choices. He is more willing to discuss the budget with people who ask respectfully and understand that not every cost is optional.
He sometimes envies people with stable careers and then reminds himself that he does not know what difficulties they may be carrying. The feeling usually passes without changing how he treats them.
A persuasive conversation is more likely to change his mind than a public argument. If he feels embarrassed or cornered, he may defend a position longer than he would in private.

His goal is not to become wealthy. He wants reliable work, decent health access, enough savings to handle an ordinary emergency, and a home life in which he and Elena are not always calculating the next bill.
